Two real bugs had to be fixed to make this testable rather than test scaffolding: build_client omitted the GitHub Enterprise /api/v3 suffix so every call against a GHE host 404s and reads as a bad token, and nothing honoured GITHUB_API_URL which octocrab does not read either - it is the variable gh honours and an operator who sets it knows their API root. The probe reads raw JSON rather than octocrab's typed Repository, because it needs one field and depending on every required field the model declares makes a response missing id report as could-not-read, a wrong answer rather than a missing one; that was not hypothetical, the first fake hit exactly that. Verified rather than assumed: the fake is driven with a real POST first and the write counter must notice, or every zero-writes assertion in the file would be true for an unrelated reason. End-to-end tests drive the real binary against a real registry of local checkouts; the maintainer case (push false, maintain true) is confirmed to report write yes. 337 tests green, 11 new.

title: Compat shim for [providers], and ro init stays deliberately dumb
description:
## The compat shim — renaming a shipped TOML table is a silent data loss

Renaming `[providers.claude]` to `[agent] engine` would **silently lose every existing user's engine configuration**, because unknown tables are ignored and `AppConfig` has no `deny_unknown_fields`. The config parses cleanly, the setting has zero effect, and nothing says so.

On load, read `[providers.claude]` and map it into `[agent] engine` **when the new key is absent**; write the new form on the next `ro config set`. **Loudly, not silently** — a deprecation note naming the old key.

The same class of hazard exists for `[identity]` gaining a `default` key, and for the per-repo `.ro/config.local.toml` `[agent] engine` → the row's `engine` column. Handle each the same way: old form read, new form written, note printed.

## ro init stays an order of magnitude simpler than it was going to be

It creates the config directory, writes the default `config.toml`, creates the database, and **prints two lines**.

There are no three modes, no `--add-dir` scan, no wizard, no PATH scan, no engine discovery, and no per-repo file to create. The onboarding verb is **`ro add`**, and it is a separate command a user runs when they mean it.

Rationale: opinionated CLI. Missing-binary errors surface lazily at `ro ship` time, not at init, and init stays about a second.

**The one thing init still does not skip:** when a per-repo file is involved elsewhere in the flow, `ro init` (or `ro add`) appends `.ro/` to `.gitignore` **idempotently** — never duplicating an existing entry, accepting `.ro/` and `/.ro/` with or without a trailing comment, never reordering or rewriting existing lines. Copy the exists-check pattern from `loader.rs::write_default` (create-if-absent, returns `Ok(false)` when present) and add the line-matching logic.

The entry is a **directory pattern**, not a filename — that is the whole reason `.ro/` exists rather than a bare `ro.local.toml`: the first thing ro later adds to that directory would otherwise start showing up as untracked.
acceptance_criteria: A legacy config with only [providers.claude] still resolves the engine. A deprecation note names the old key. ro init writes the config and DB and prints two lines, with no scanning. The .ro/ gitignore entry is added once and never duplicated.
close_reason: Landed. resolved_engine takes agent.engine when present and falls back to the legacy providers table otherwise; engine_deprecation_note says so on load, naming the old key and the exact command that writes the new form. The new key wins when both are present, so a stale providers.claude cannot make the new key unsettable. The old table had one entry per provider rather than one engine setting, so which-engine-this was inferred from which entry had a binary in it; that inference is the entire back-compat surface, so it lives in one named function returning the key it fired on, which is what lets the note say providers.claude rather than providers. The default template stopped shipping providers.*: had it kept them, every new user would open their own config and be told they were using something deprecated on day zero, and a test now asserts the table is absent for that reason. The gitignore half of this bead is not done: it is conditioned on the per-repo .ro/config.local.toml file, which Phase 1 cut, so there is nothing to add the entry for yet. It lands with the per-repo file. 299 tests green, 4 new for the shim.

title: Phase 4 — ro-engine crate and the atomic sweep cut
description:
## Goal

The core reversal lands — an engine abstraction with a hard boundary — **and the command it replaces dies in the same commit that guts it**.

## The boundary that makes the identity guarantees real

**The engine commits. `ro` pushes.** The engine reads the diff, groups the work, writes the commits, and resolves conflicts. It does not push, does not open a PR, does not create a branch, and **never sees a credential**.

An earlier draft injected the resolved token into the engine's environment. That was wrong, and the correction is its own bead. Every guarantee in the auth design depends on this boundary: if the engine pushes, the extraheader, `expected_login`, `SecretString` and per-repo identity all become advice given to a process that is free to ignore it.

## Why the sweep cut is ATOMIC and lives here

`Bucket::classify` / `is_test` / `is_doc` / `is_config` / `prefix` / `scope_of` / `task_id_of` and the conventional-commit template are the **only** producer of `PlannedCommit { bucket, message, files }` — `commit_sweep.rs:372` assigns the bucket and `:382` builds the message.

Delete them and `plan_repo` cannot construct a plan, leaving `ro sweep commit-sweep` **compiled but semantically hollow** while Phase 1j keeps it alive. The old path must die in the same commit as the code that powered it, and Phase 4's verification must **run the CLI**, not just unit tests.

## Done looks like

Conventional-commit bucketing is gone from the tree, three engines implement one trait, a missing `claude` surfaces as a per-repo error at dispatch rather than a process exit, and there is exactly one fleet-commit path left in the codebase.
acceptance_criteria: ro sweep is gone. ro --help lists the intended surface. ro-engine exists with three built-ins. The Bucket classifier is deleted in the same commit as the namespace. CLI smoke tests pass, not just unit tests.

title: Create crates/ro-engine with the Engine trait
acceptance_criteria: crates/ro-engine compiles as a lib with no clap or tokio. All three manifest edits are in one commit. The trait is declared exactly once in the tree. EngineOutcome is a value type.
close_reason: Landed as 6d14ee7. New crate ro-engine: Engine trait (Send+Sync), EngineKind with exactly three slots, Availability, CommitRecord, EngineContext, and EngineOutcome. EngineOutcome is a VALUE not a Result - a Result invites ? inside a worker and one escaping ? converts a per-repo failure into a fleet abort; an enum has no error channel to write ? into. Availability and TimedOut are separate variants because a bare Failed cannot distinguish a normal error from a killed child. GitEngine is the raw backend, never the default, with an explicit wip-on-<branch> message rather than a generated conventional commit. Three manifest edits in one commit. No clap, no tokio - verified in the dependency tree. Negative control: stage_all as a no-op turns 3 tests red. Changing add -A to add . leaves them green, because git 2.x reconciled the flags; the test pins the behaviour and the doc says so rather than claiming a distinction it cannot make.

title: End-to-end test: two repos, two authors and two accounts, one command
description:
## The capability under test

The developer has a work account and a personal one. In one fleet run, repo A commits as the work identity and pushes with the work credential; repo B commits as the personal identity and pushes with the personal credential. **That is the reason the tool exists** — without it, the daily loop still needs a terminal per repo to switch identity.

## The test

A fixture with repo A (`author_ref = work`, `credential_ref = env:WORK_TOKEN`) and repo B (`author_ref = personal`, `credential_ref = env:PERSONAL_TOKEN`). Run one `ro ship --execute`.

Assert:

- `git log -1 --format='%ae'` in A is the work email; in B, the personal one.
- Each push carried its own credential — the bare remotes record which account reached them.
- **Neither repo's `.git/config` was written.** Identity is applied per invocation via `GIT_CONFIG_*` and `-c`, so a per-repo author does not leak into the user's global config or into a sibling repo.
- A repo with `author_ref = NULL` and a global `[identity] default` uses the default — so **adding a global identity upgrades every existing repo without touching a row.**
- A repo with no `[identity]` block at all falls back to git's own configured user, unchanged.
- `expected_login` mismatch aborts that repo **before** any push, even though the commit author is correct. This is the field separation: the author is controlled, the pushing account is not.

## The regression this test exists to prevent

A test in an earlier revision of the plan asserted two repos committing as two different people **while the schema had no per-repo author column** — it could not fail, because the capability it described had been removed in an earlier round. **A test that cannot fail is worse than no test.**

This one is written against `author_ref`, which exists.
acceptance_criteria: One ship run, two authors, two credentials, neither .git/config written. NULL author_ref follows the global default. expected_login mismatch aborts before the push even with a correct author.

title: GitEngine: the raw backend and the explicit fallback, never the default
description:
## What it does

`stage_all` -> `commit_all` with a single message (the `--message` flag, or a generic fallback). It never spawns a second process to invent a message.

## Why it is NOT the default

It **cannot read the diff, split commits, or resolve conflicts** — which is exactly why the agent engines exist. The vision names three built-ins and says only claude, codex, and git ship; of those, `git` is the honest floor, not the product.

An earlier draft had this backwards and made the deterministic bucketing the headline. That was ro reimplementing, badly, what a model does for free.

## It needs primitives that did not exist before Phase 3

`mutation::commit` refuses an empty file list and explicitly forbids `add -A`, so **WIP-style "commit everything" is impossible through the typed API today** — which is why `ro-sweep/src/commit.rs:110-140` hand-rolls it in violation of ro-git's own stated rule. Phase 3 adds `stage_all` / `commit_all`; this bead is where they get used.

## Tests

- `GitEngine` on a dirty repo containing a **brand-new untracked directory** produces one commit containing that directory's files (the `-uall` behaviour).
- A clean repo returns `NothingToCommit`, counted as ok, with no push attempted.
- The commit subject is the `--message` value when supplied and a stable generic string when not.
acceptance_criteria: GitEngine commits a brand-new untracked directory in one commit. NothingToCommit on a clean repo. No subprocess spawned to invent a message. It is selectable but is not the default.

title: Claude and Codex engines, and the prompt that must not say push
description:
## What they are

Thin wrappers: spawn `bin` + `args` in `repo_root` with the injected env, capture stdout/stderr, **parse the commit list out of the stream**, enforce a hard timeout, and kill the child tree on expiry.

No prompt-engineering sophistication lives here. The contract is *"hand the worktree to the agent, get commits back"*.

## The built-in prompt, and the sentence that must not change

```
Read the full diff of this repository. Group the changes into a small
number of logically connected commits, in dependency order, and write
each one with a specific subject line describing what that commit
actually does.

Do not edit any source file. Do not reformat. Do not add obviously
ephemeral files (build output, lockfiles from an unrelated package,
scratch notes, editor backups).

Do not push, and do not run any command that contacts the remote. Do
not modify git config — not `git config --local`, not `git config
--global`. Your author identity is already set for you; the caller
handles the credential, the remote, and the push.
```

**"Do not push" is the load-bearing line.** Prompt examples that end "commit all changed files and then push" are common, and following one puts the credential in a transcript. The line is there because the natural instinct is the opposite.

**"Do not modify git config" is a request, not a control** — the control is that ro re-asserts `-c user.name=… -c user.email=…` on every commit it performs, so a `git config --local user.email x` from the engine changes nothing ro later does. ro also hashes `.git/config` before dispatch and after, and **warns** if it changed: not to undo it, but because an agent writing git config is something the user needs to know happened.

## `{prompt}` is substituted as ONE argv element, never through a shell

The prompt is built from diff text and file paths. Passing any of it through a shell is a **command-injection path into the user's own account**.

## Tests

- A missing binary yields `Unavailable` naming the binary, **without a non-zero process exit** — the other repos in the fleet still commit and the run exits 1.
- An engine that hangs is killed at the timeout and reported as `TimedOut`, not `Failed`, and the fleet completes.
- A non-zero agent exit is classified into the shared `FailureClass` — one taxonomy, not two.
- The built-in prompt contains no instruction to push. Assert on the literal string, so the regression is caught at the source rather than in a behavioural test a sufficiently literal agent could route around.
acceptance_criteria: Both engines spawn, parse commits, and time out correctly. The built-in prompt contains no push instruction. {prompt} is one argv element. A missing binary is a per-repo Unavailable, not an exit.

title: The engine's environment is built by SUBTRACTION, not addition
description:
## This bead corrects a real defect in an earlier revision of the plan

The earlier text said the resolved token was injected into the engine's environment alongside `GH_TOKEN` for the agent's own use. **That is a leak with a long fuse**, and every step of it is outside ro's control:

```
1. ro spawns claude with GH_TOKEN in its environment
2. the agent runs `env`, or printenv, or a build script, or a crash reporter
3. the value lands in the agent's stdout
4. the agent's stdout lands in its transcript, which is written to disk
5. the transcript is uploaded, pasted into an issue, or read by a different
   model on the next session
```

There is no point in that chain where ro can intervene, and the destination is frequently a third party. A credential is exactly the kind of thing that must not be in an LLM's context: not because the model is careless, but because **the transcript is designed to be read and shared**, which is the opposite of a secret store.

`SecretString` protects ro's own logs and panics. It cannot protect a file ro does not write.

## The fix — assemble by subtraction

```
child_env = parent_env
             .remove(GH_TOKEN)
             .remove(GITHUB_TOKEN)
             .remove(RO_CREDENTIAL)         // if such a var is ever set
             .set(GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT, "0")
             .set(GCM_INTERACTIVE, "Never")
             .set(GIT_PAGER, "cat")
             .set(GIT_CONFIG_*, identity)   // from [identity.<profile>]
             // + any explicit EngineContext.env
```

**Stripping is mandatory, not merely adding-nothing.** A user who has `GH_TOKEN` exported in their shell for `gh` would otherwise hand it to every agent ro spawns, with neither of them intending it.

## The author DOES reach the engine, deliberately

If the engine runs `git commit`, git needs an identity from its environment or its config, and **there is no third place to put it.** Passing `GIT_AUTHOR_*` is unavoidable.

It is also not a secret — it is about to be in a public commit. What matters is that the engine must not *choose* it, which is handled in two layers: ro exports the identity on the child's environment, and ro re-asserts `-c` on every commit it performs.

**Use `GIT_CONFIG_*`, not `GIT_AUTHOR_*`** — it covers `commit --amend`, `tag`, and every other object-creating call, four variables become two, and it is the same mechanism as the `-c` ro already passes. Note honestly: **the agent can still read it with `printenv`**, and pretending otherwise is worse than saying so.

## No remote rewrite, therefore nothing to restore

An alternative design would `git remote set-url` to a credential-bearing URL, push, then restore. That has a second thing that can fail, needs a `finally`, can be killed between its halves, and puts a credential into an on-disk file for the duration. `git -c …extraheader=…` writes nothing: **no window in which a token exists on disk, and therefore no restore to forget.**

## Tests

- Export `GH_TOKEN` in the harness, dispatch the fake engine, assert the value appears in **neither** the engine's env, **nor** its argv, **nor** its captured stdout/stderr.
- The fake engine runs `printenv` and echoes everything back; assert no value matches `ghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}` or `github_pat_…`.
- A repo with **no** `[auth] credential` still gets a child env with no `GH_TOKEN` — stripping is **unconditional**, not conditional on there being a credential to protect.
- `GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL` reaches the engine, and `GIT_CONFIG_*` covers `commit --amend` too.
acceptance_criteria: GH_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN are removed from the child env unconditionally. No PAT-shaped value appears anywhere in the engine's env, argv, or output. The author is present via GIT_CONFIG_*. No remote is ever rewritten, so there is no restore path to forget.

title: Engine discovery and lazy availability, with three fixed slots
description:
## Availability is checked at DISPATCH time only

Not at `ro init`. **Not at `ro doctor`.** This is a single rule with no exception: doctor stays a fast environment check, and `check_provider` is already `Severity::Optional` so it can only ever warn.

A missing engine is an `EngineOutcome::Unavailable` **for one repo** — a per-repo failure, not a fleet abort. A user with neither claude nor codex installed gets a loud per-repo message telling them to set `[agent] engine = "git"`, not a silent skip.

## Three fixed slots, NOT a free-form table

A user-editable `[engines.*]` table reintroduces exactly the silent-failure class the config section exists to kill: `engines.cladue.bin = "claude"` parses cleanly, registers a **phantom engine**, and fails at dispatch. The user typed one wrong character and spent an afternoon.

Instead — three fixed slots, each its own `deny_unknown_fields` struct, plus a per-run binary override for the "installed under an unusual name" case:

```toml
[engine_claude]
bin = "claude"
default_args = ["-p", "--output-format", "stream-json"]
[engine_codex]
bin = "codex"
default_args = ["exec"]
[engine_git]
bin = "git"
default_args = []
```

```
ro ship --engine claude --engine-bin /opt/bin/claude-nightly
```

## This is how a fourth agent gets added without a ro release

`[agent] command` overrides the binary and its arguments entirely, and `[agent] prompt` replaces the instruction — so Gemini, Amp, Kiro, or a nightly build is **a config change, not a PR**. It is not a plugin registry: the registry of *behaviour profiles* is a fixed three-entry array, and the two strings are the extensibility.

**It cannot relax the agent-does-not-push boundary.** Whatever binary is named, ro still owns the push, so the credential and the identity guard still apply to it.

## The PATH probe belongs in ro-git

`which_in` is currently at `crates/ro/src/doctor.rs:392` inside `mod doctor;` in the `ro` **binary** crate, so a new **library** crate cannot call it. Move it to ro-git — it is a subprocess PATH probe, which is what ro-git is — and have both doctor and the engines call it there. It already handles the Windows `.exe` suffix.

## Test

A registry-free dispatch-table test proves adding a fourth engine is one `impl` plus one match arm, with no change to the orchestrator, the config resolver, or the CLI.
acceptance_criteria: Availability is probed at dispatch only. Three fixed slots reject a typo'd key. --engine-bin overrides a binary for one run. A missing engine is a per-repo Unavailable. which_in lives in ro-git and is callable from a library.

title: Delete the ro sweep namespace atomically with the Bucket classifier
description:
## Same commit — all of it

- `Bucket::classify` / `is_test` / `is_doc` / `is_config` / `prefix` / `scope_of` / `task_id_of` and the conventional-commit message template
- `SweepCommands` (`crates/ro/src/main.rs:307-378`)
- the three handler arms (`:1043-1304`)
- `AutoApproveLevel` (`:37-43`)
- `commit.rs`, `agent.rs` (**a module named "agent" that spawns no agent and never sets `applied = true`**), `risk.rs`, `policy_check.rs` (zero CLI callers)

## Why it MUST be atomic

`Bucket::classify` is the **only** producer of `PlannedCommit { bucket, message, files }` — `commit_sweep.rs:372` assigns the bucket, `:382` builds the message. Delete the classifier and `plan_repo` cannot construct a plan, leaving `ro sweep commit-sweep` **compiled but semantically hollow** while Phase 1j keeps it alive.

The old path dies in the same commit as the code that powered it. **Never leave the flagship command alive-but-gutted** — it is the command the CLI is judged on, and a hollow version ships as a silent failure.

## KEEP — carry these over, do not re-derive

- the NUL-safe `parse_porcelain` -> into ro-engine
- the `-uall` decision plus the **nested-repo trailing-`/` guard** -> into ro-engine
- `is_protected_branch` -> into ro-engine
- `denylist.rs` **verbatim** -> stays in ro-sweep
- `secret_scan.rs` with its unreachable-branch fix -> stays in ro-sweep
- `quality_gates.rs` as opt-in -> stays in ro-sweep

**The crate keeps its name.** Renaming `ro-sweep` to `ro-safety` is churn that buys nothing and breaks the workspace path in a dozen places.

## Manifest

`ro-sweep/Cargo.toml` drops `ro-core`, `ro-jobs`, `ro-output`, `tokio`, `comfy-table`, `ro-config`, `serde_yaml`, `ro-state`, `rusqlite`, and the duplicate `tempfile`.

## ro doctor is LEFT ALONE — do not add probes

An earlier revision contradicted itself: availability checked at dispatch only, then a `gh` probe added to doctor two paragraphs later. **Do not add probes.** `check_provider` is already `Severity::Optional` (`doctor.rs:372`) so it can only warn and cannot change `DoctorReport::exit_code()`. The docs should say that. Two tests need **comment** updates, not behaviour changes: `doctor.rs:562` asserts `>= 6` checks (still true) and `doctor.rs:536` asserts `Severity::Optional` (still true).

## Verification must run the CLI, not just unit tests

- `ro sweep` is gone; `ro --help` lists the intended surface
- `--filter tag:x` no longer matches every repo
- an invalid `--repos` glob **errors** instead of silently selecting the whole fleet
acceptance_criteria: No Bucket/classify remains. ro sweep namespace gone in the same commit. parse_porcelain, the nested-repo guard, is_protected_branch, denylist, secret_scan and quality_gates are carried over. doctor is unchanged. CLI smoke tests pass.
prerequisites: ro-engine-crate-and-trait — the carried-over code has a new home.

title: Test infrastructure: fake gh, fake engines, multi-repo bare remotes
description:
## Why this is early and why it blocks

Almost every test in the plan needs to stand up a fake `gh`, a fake engine binary, or a bare remote, and several of them need the same ones. Building that ad hoc per test produces fixtures that disagree with each other and a suite that passes for the wrong reason.

## The cross-platform shim problem

**A shell script is not directly executable on Windows.** Write a **`gh.cmd` shim** on Windows and a `gh` shell script elsewhere, and put the containing directory **first on `PATH`** for the test process. A fixture that only works on Unix is a fixture that silently does not run on two thirds of the CI matrix.

The same for engine binaries (`claude`, `codex`).

## Bare remotes

Multi-repo tests need real remotes, not mocks: `git init --bare` per repo, then clone. A mocked `git push` cannot assert **that the push went out over the wrong identity**, which is the failure mode the entire credential design exists to prevent.

Keep **two** bare remotes per fixture: one the credential is expected to reach, and a second that verifies the engine's *own* push attempt did **not** reach it. That pair is what makes the engine-does-not-push test meaningful.

## The shim must record invocations

Every fake records its argv, its environment, and the bare remotes it saw writes against, to a file the test reads back. Asserting the `Command` was *built* with something is not enough — the failure mode being designed against is a variable that is set but never seen, and a push that was attempted but went to the wrong remote.

## Log capture

A helper that captures everything ro wrote to stdout and stderr during a run, for the leak-chain tests and for asserting a `***` rendering.

## Scope

Build this before Phase 3's credential work, not alongside it — three of the four dedicated test beads depend on it.
acceptance_criteria: A fake gh that works on Windows and Unix, driven by PATH. Fake claude/codex recording argv, env and writes. Two bare remotes per fixture. Captured stdout/stderr per run. Used by at least the credential, leak-chain and identity-isolation tests.
close_reason: Landed as 2e89365. New crate ro-testkit: FakeBinary (gh/claude/codex shims, cross-platform gh vs gh.cmd via PATHEXT, recording argv to a log the test reads back), BareRemote + RemotePair (two real bare repos, so 'the engine did not push' is distinguishable from 'the engine had nowhere to push'), Worktree (clean/dirty, files inside a brand-new untracked directory), Captured (both streams, PAT-shaped predicate, truncated failure output). No workspace dependency, so it can fake gh for ro-github's own tests. TestEnv installs shim + env under one lock and restores inside catch_unwind, so nesting is inexpressible and a panic cannot leave PATH swapped. 15 self-tests, verified by blinding the recorder: the_recorder_is_not_blind and a_shim_really_runs_and_records_its_argv go red, 13 stay green.

title: Test V4 and V5 against a database created by the previous binary
description:
## This is the ONLY test that can catch a stale column read

`ALTER TABLE repos DROP COLUMN default_branch` succeeds. The migration succeeds. `cargo test` is **green** — because a freshly-built test database never had the column in the first place, so a `SELECT` left behind **compiles fine**.

Then every existing user's `ro push` fails at runtime with "no such column".

The fix is one test: build a database with the **previous** binary (or by running the migrations up to V3), then run the current binary against it.

## What it must cover

- Open a `state.db` created by the **pre-V4** binary, apply V4, then run `ro remove` and `ro prune` against it. This is the ONLY proof the V4 path works, because a fresh DB skips it entirely.
- The same for V5: a pre-V5 database upgrades, and **every existing row has `credential_ref IS NULL` and `author_ref IS NULL`** — i.e. every existing repo keeps the global credential. That is the correct back-compat behaviour, not merely the absence of a migration.
- `ro push` and `ro status` still work against the upgraded database.
- **V5 is idempotent.** `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN` is **not** idempotent in SQLite and errors with `duplicate column name` on a second run. Guard it like the existing `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` migrations. This is the most likely way a migration like this ships broken: the second run of ro on an upgraded machine fails at open.
- A `SELECT` that enumerated `repos` columns before V5 does not silently return nulls for the new columns — `manage::add` inserts a fixed list (`migrate.rs:331,337`) and `manage::list` selects a `REPO_COLUMNS` constant, and a stale enumeration is a wrong answer, not a compile error.

## Why this is P0

Both migrations are forward-only and neither is covered by the normal test path. The plan's own V4 checklist says "grep the name before migrating" — a test does that grep **permanently**.
acceptance_criteria: A pre-V4 and a pre-V5 database both upgrade and ro remove, ro prune, ro push and ro status work against them. V5 run twice does not error. Existing rows keep the global credential.

title: End-to-end test: the credential never reaches the agent
description:
## The guarantee, stated so the test can be written against it

The resolved credential exists in exactly two places: ro's memory, and the argv of the one `git` invocation that pushes. It exists **nowhere** the agent can observe — not in the child's environment, not in its argv, not in its stdout, and therefore not in its transcript.

## The test

Run a full `ro ship --execute` across a fixture with two repos and two different credentials, with a fake `claude` that:
1. dumps its entire environment (`printenv`)
2. dumps its argv
3. writes its full stdout and stderr to a file
4. **attempts a `git push` of its own** to the wrong bare remote

Then assert:

- Neither credential appears in the engine's env, argv, stdout, stderr, or the transcript file.
- No value in the captured output matches `ghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}` or `github_pat_…`.
- The engine's own push attempt did **not** reach the credentialed remote.
- ro's push **did** reach it, and the bare remote's reflog shows it carried the extraheader.
- The captured ro stdout/stderr contains no PAT-shaped string — a `SecretString` whose `Debug` renders `***`, asserted through a real run rather than a unit test.
- The two repos pushed as **two different accounts**, each with its own expected credential.

## Why this is the headline test

It is the only test that exercises the whole chain — resolver, env subtraction, prompt, spawn, capture, push — rather than one link. Every individual link can be right while the chain leaks, and the chain is the thing an LLM's transcript makes dangerous in a way no other credential in the tool is.
acceptance_criteria: A full two-repo run with two credentials produces zero PAT-shaped strings in any engine output, and the engine's own push reaches neither remote. ro's push reaches the right remote with the right credential on each.

title: Phase 5 — ro ship, ro push, ro commit and the surface
description:
## Goal

The three verbs that replace the daily Git workflow ship, and the surface matches the vision.

## The daily loop this produces

```bash
ro add          # once per repo
ro sync         # morning: clone what is missing, fetch, pull --rebase
# ... code all day ...
ro status       # which are dirty
ro ship         # AI commits, ro pushes. One word.
```

Splitting further is for when you want them separately: `ro commit`, read `git log`, then `ro push`.

## One pipeline, three entry points

`ro commit` and `ro push` are the same per-repo pipeline with a different **stopping point**, and keeping them one function is what stops the two from drifting.

- `ro commit` runs steps **a-g** and returns.
- `ro push` runs **a-h**.
- `ro ship` runs **a-h** too — it is the two in one word, **not a new pipeline**.
- `ro sync` is a **different pipeline entirely**, because it must not touch the index or spawn anything.

An earlier revision split this into `ro checkpoint`, `ro pr` and `ro conflict`, and the split was wrong in a specific way rather than merely excessive: the first verb always had to know whether the others were coming, and *"I have work and I want it off my machine now"* is all of it at once.

## What is NOT in this phase, deliberately

- **No pull requests.** Cut three times. A PR is a request for someone else's attention on a branch meant to last; this tool's premise is a fire drill across a fleet. It took `gh pr create`/`gh pr list`, the `ro/wip/*` branch, six PR flags, and `gh` as a push-path dependency with it. The rebase base survives, because the rebase needs one.
- **No `ro conflict` verb.** Conflict resolution is a stage inside `ro push` behind `--resolve`. An interactive command over twenty repos is not a command.
- **No `ro run`, and run history is NOT wired.** `ro_jobs::open_run`/`append_event`/`finalize_run` have **zero production callers** today — they exist, they are tested, and nothing calls them, which is exactly the kind of thing that looks like a feature and is not one. With no verb to read the rows with, and a database nobody queries not being an audit trail, the answer is **do not wire them.** The per-repo stdout summary replaces it. Say so in the code, so the next person does not helpfully connect them.
- **No WIP branch.** `ro push` pushes the branch you are on, and refuses on a protected branch rather than inventing a name.

## Done looks like

Ten commands in three tiers, four modules, five migrations, no review, no `ro health` command, no fork, no sweep, no import, no self-update, no `ro repos` namespace, no pull requests, no toon, and **every documented claim true**.
acceptance_criteria: All child beads green. ro help lists exactly the ten commands. A live three-repo fleet run with one deliberately failing repo exits 1. ro sync --dry-run prints a per-repo summary naming the account each credential resolved to.

title: One positional target resolver, registry-scoped, never a filesystem scan
description:
## The rule

```bash
ro ship                      # every repo in the registry
ro ship cass                 # one
ro ship cass voice-ai-agent  # several
```

One `resolve_targets(&[String]) -> Result<Vec<Repo>>` in `ro-sync::targets` accepts a **bare name, an alias, or `owner/name`**, and is used by `sync`, `commit`, `push` and `ship` so they **cannot disagree about what a name means**.

**An empty list means every row in the registry** — resolved from the database.

## The safety property

The set of repos ro will **push with the user's credential** must never depend on where they happen to be standing. An empty list is a database query, not a directory walk. Nothing is ever discovered by scanning.

A name that matches two repos is an **ambiguity error listing both**, not a coin flip.

## Lifted from `resolve_multi_repo_targets` (main.rs:554-611) with four fixes

- The `has:` bool-expression bug
- The invalid-glob-becomes-`*` bug: an invalid `--repos` glob **errors** instead of silently selecting the whole fleet
- `archived = 0 AND disabled = 0` added — today `manage::list` (`ro-sync/src/manage.rs:208-210`) has **no WHERE on either**, so `--all` selects repos the user explicitly archived or disabled. This is a fleet-correctness bug the flagship command would inherit.
- A real `repo_tags` reader. Today `--filter tag:orch` does `label.contains(rest)` against the literal string `owner/name`, so it silently selects every repo whose owner or name contains "orch".

## A registered-but-uncloned row is skipped, not cloned mid-transaction

Skip with reason `NotCloned` and print `ro add <url>` as the fix. Cloning inside `ro sync` is safe — idempotent, known-empty target. Cloning partway through a commit-and-push loop, because of a typo in a local path, pulls a repository over the network in the middle of a transaction.

## collect_git_dirs must be made public

It is a **private** `fn collect_git_dirs(dir, depth, out)` at `ro-sync/src/prune.rs:163`, with `const MAX_DEPTH: usize = 4` at `:164`, and `ro-sync/src/lib.rs` has no re-export. The only public entry is `find_orphans`, which is coupled to SQLite and returns `Vec<Orphan>` **after** the tracked-path comparison — routing anything read-only through it routes the call through the database *and* through the exact code Phase 1 is repairing. Make the walker `pub` (or move it to `ro-git::discover_dirs`) and turn `MAX_DEPTH` into a parameter.

## Tests

A bare name, an alias, and `owner/name` all resolve, and all three verbs agree. An unknown name is a **64** (usage error), not an empty run. `ro ship --all` on an empty inventory is a legitimate **0**. An archived or disabled repo is excluded by default and included with `--include-archived`. A name matching two repos is an ambiguity error naming both. A `.git` directory sitting next to a managed one, never registered, is absent from the target set — **even if it has a `.ro/config.local.toml`**, because a file cannot grant management.
acceptance_criteria: Empty selector = the registry, never a scan. Four bugs fixed (has:, glob, archived filter, tag match). Ambiguity is an error. Uncloned rows skip. The no-scan test passes.

title: Fix the sync FK bug and the failed-pull-recorded-as-success bug
description:
## Two silent failures in the sync path

**1. `sync_results` is permanently empty.** `sync_all` mints `run_id = Uuid::new_v4()` at `ro-sync/src/sync.rs:306` and never inserts a `runs` row, but `sync_results.run_id` is `NOT NULL REFERENCES runs(id)` and `ro_state::open_db` sets `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON`. The insert **fails and is swallowed** by `let _ = conn.execute(…)` at `sync.rs:326`.

Consequences: `sync_results` empty forever, `ro status`'s `last_synced_at` permanently NULL, and the health scorer's failed-sync penalty permanently zero — so a repo that fails to sync **scores as healthy**. Fix: thread a real id through.

**2. A failed pull is recorded as a success.** The pull branch never checks `outcome.result.ok()` — the clone branch immediately above it does — and `PullOutcome::conflict` is computed and then discarded. So a conflicted `--rebase` pull lands in `sync_results` as `updated` / `success` / `error: None`.

This is the same class as the health-score cut: **a number that is always zero when it cannot be computed, and always success when it failed**, is worse than no number. Fix both, and make the standalone `rebase` primitive from Phase 3 return a distinguishable outcome the caller can branch on.

## Also in this bead

- Add the `archived` / `disabled` filter to `sync_all` — the same fleet-correctness bug the target resolver gets, inherited by the sync loop.
- Wire `-j` and `--timeout` to **real** executors. Today `--timeout` is worse than a no-op: `SyncOptions.timeout_secs` is set at `main.rs:739` and **never read anywhere** in `ro-sync/src/sync.rs` — only the struct field at `:40` and the `Default` impl at `:54`. It is a hardcoded literal that never consults `[core].timeout_secs`.
- Delete `--resume`. There is no daemon to resume into, and a flag that claims to resume is a promise the tool does not keep.

## Tests

- A successful sync makes `last_synced_at` non-NULL — the FK regression.
- A **failed** pull records a failure, not success.
- A **conflicted** rebase records the conflict, not `updated`.
- A health snapshot for a repo whose sync failed has a non-zero penalty — the health scorer is only correct if the penalty is reachable.
acceptance_criteria: sync_results is populated. A failed or conflicted pull is not recorded as success. The archived/disabled filter applies. -j and --timeout do something. --resume is gone.

title: Rewrite the cli_init integration tests against the ten-command surface
description:
## The starting position

`crates/ro/tests/cli_init.rs` has **five tests and it is the only integration test file in the entire workspace.** Every one of them hardcodes the flat surface — `ro init`, `ro add`, `ro list --format json`, `ro remove`, `ro import` — and `ro import` is deleted in Phase 1, so all five break.

The test struct is still named **`RfoTest`** from the pre-rename era (`rfo`). Rename it.

## What the rewritten tests should cover

- `ro init` creates the config dir and database; running it twice is idempotent.
- `ro add` on a local path registers a row; on a URL it clones; a failed clone writes **no** row.
- `ro list --format json` emits a parseable array with the ten commands' data shape.
- `ro remove` cascades dependent rows and is refused for an unknown key with a usage error.
- `ro status` distinguishes clean / dirty / ahead / behind / conflict per repo, and an **unknown** state for an unmeasurable one.
- `ro ship --dry-run` prints a plan and **changes nothing** — no commit, no push, no engine spawned. Assert the fake engine's invocation log is empty.

## Cross-platform

The suite runs on a 3-OS matrix. Any fixture that assumes a POSIX shell or `/tmp` is a test that silently does not run on Windows. Use `tempfile`, and the `gh.cmd` / `gh` shim approach from the test-infrastructure bead.

## Do not write these as unit tests

The value here is the **CLI surface**: argument parsing, exit codes, and the actual binary. A unit test on a handler proves the handler, not the tool.
acceptance_criteria: All five original tests rewritten against the ten commands, or replaced. RfoTest renamed. Windows and Unix both pass. ro ship --dry-run proves no engine is spawned.

title: Rewrite README.md and FEATURES.md against reality
description:
## Both files have drifted from the code

`FEATURES.md` documents flags that do not exist and commands that are being deleted:

- `ro review plan --format json` — no such flag; `repo` was a required positional
- `ro fork sync` flags that never existed
- `ro robot-docs all` — a topic that never existed
- the run-recording claim, for a feature that is not being wired
- the `--parallel` / `--resume` / `--verbose` no-ops
- `ro self-update` "Replace[s] the installed binary" — it never could

A rewrite against reality, not a patch of the list above: the docs must be derivable from the clap tree so they cannot drift again. `ro schema` exists precisely so an agent can read the truth instead of the prose.

## Must PRESERVE

- `README.md:415-417` — the no-outside-contributions policy.
- The `ro-illustration.webp` reference.
- The install instructions that `ro self-update` used to print.

## The install-script bugs this surfaced

- `install.ps1:138` claims config lives at `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ro\config.toml`. `ro init` actually writes it to `%APPDATA%` (Roaming) via `dirs::config_dir()`, and `state.db` to `%LOCALAPPDATA%`.
- `install.sh:234-236` warns *"set `RO_FORCE=0` to refuse"* when `0` is already the default and the install is unconditional.

## The new README leads with the daily loop

```bash
ro add && ro sync
# ... code ...
ro ship
```

Then the ten commands, then what ro deliberately does **not** do: no daemon, no cloud, no workspace entity, no pull requests, no TUI, no auto-discovery. The negative list is load-bearing — a user who assumes a daemon exists will wait for one.

## Test

A check that every command named in README and FEATURES exists in `ro --help`, and vice versa. That is the only thing that stops the drift from recurring, and it is roughly twenty lines.
acceptance_criteria: Both docs describe the ten commands accurately. Preserved sections intact. install scripts' path claims fixed. A test asserts the docs and the clap tree agree in both directions.

title: Alias the removed command names for one release
description:
## There are ZERO aliases anywhere in the current clap tree

So nothing is in the way — and the four most-used commands in the tool (`ro add`, `ro list`, `ro remove`, `ro status`) are not being moved, so they need no alias themselves.

**What needs an alias is what is being removed**, and the biggest one is on the daily path of anyone already using this tool:

| Removed | Replacement |
|---|---|
| `ro sweep commit-sweep --all --execute` | `ro ship --execute` — a hidden `#[command(alias = …)]`, printing a deprecation line naming the replacement. This is the **single most-used invocation today.** |
| `ro status` | `ro status` — stays; no alias needed |
| `ro health` | `ro list` — hidden alias, one release |
| `ro robot-docs` | `ro schema` — hidden alias, one release |
| `ro import`, `ro prune`, `ro self-update`, `ro fork`, `ro review` | *(gone — a release-note table mapping old to new)* |

## An alias must live on the NEW command

So the old flat spelling keeps working. The top-level `Commands::Add` etc. become hidden `#[command(alias = "…")]` pass-throughs in the same commit.

## State a removal version, in the release notes AND the docs

**An alias with no announced removal is an indefinite compatibility tax.** This is a bigger break than the exit-code redefinition and deserves the same treatment, not less.

Print a deprecation line to **stderr** naming the replacement, so it does not corrupt stdout for anything parsing the output.

## Test

Each aliased invocation produces the same result as its replacement, exits with the same code, and prints a deprecation line naming the replacement and the removal version.
acceptance_criteria: Every removed daily-path command has a one-release alias. Deprecation lines go to stderr and name the replacement. A removal version is stated in the release notes and the docs. A test runs each alias and compares it to its replacement.

title: crates/ro/src/ship — one module, three entry points
description:
## New

`crates/ro/src/ship/{mod,orchestrator,emit,summary}.rs`, serving **all three** entry points, parameterised by how far the pipeline runs. The orchestrator lives in the `ro` binary — a two-crate split mints a hard cross-crate boundary for very little, and its own trait sketch already showed the symptom.

## The per-repo steps

```
a. lock      RepoLock::acquire_at(state_dir/locks/<hex>.lock, t)
b. preflight conflict::detect -> Skip
             is_dirty -> (commit: Skip if clean)
             denylist + secret_scan -> Block      BEFORE the engine runs
c. config    resolve_effective(.ro/config.local.toml, row, global)  [no DB]
d. identity  GIT_CONFIG_* from the row's author_ref
 e. base      git fetch
f. engine    engine.checkpoint(ctx)              <- ro commit returns here
g. push      git push; credential per AuthPolicy
h. unlock
 i. RepoOutcome  (value; ? becomes Failed)
```

## Per-repo independence is a VALUE return, not a Result

`ro_sync::sync::sync_repo` already models this correctly; `ro_sync::status::status_all` does **not** — it uses `?` on `status_repo` and aborts the whole fleet on one corrupt working copy (`ro-sync/src/status.rs:90+`). **Do not copy the second one.**

## The coordinator owns all DB access

`rusqlite::Connection` is `!Sync` — it contains `RefCell<InnerConnection>`. `std::thread::scope` **cannot** share one, and the attempt fails with E0277. So: **workers touch only git and the filesystem; the coordinator thread does every DB read and write.** WAL mode and `busy_timeout=5000` are already set in `ro-state/src/lib.rs:48-58` for exactly this. This is the required shape, not an implementation detail.

## The scan happens once, on the coordinator, before any worker

`main.rs:1216-1300` today plans every repo in loop 1, prints, then applies in loop 2. Once an engine can mutate a worktree, a plan computed in loop 1 is **stale by loop 2**. One status scan up front removes the staleness without persisting a plan artifact, and it is what makes `base_branch` trustworthy.

## Workers

`std::thread::scope` with a bounded count from `[core] parallel`. No async runtime — the git layer is synchronous and stays that way. The declared `tokio` dependency has zero references and should be removed from the manifests rather than wired up.

## Test

A three-repo fixture with one deliberately failing repo: the other two still commit and push, the run exits **1**, and the summary names the failure with its cause. A failing repo must not stop or roll back the others.
acceptance_criteria: One module serves commit, push and ship. Workers never touch the DB. The scan is taken once. A three-repo run with one failure commits the other two and exits 1.

title: Rebase BEFORE the engine, so the happy path never force-pushes
description:
## The ordering, and why it is not the conventional one

The conventional order is `commit -> push -> rejected -> rebase -> force-push`. It rewrites the branch, so the push needs `--force-with-lease`, and **a force-push across a fleet is the one operation here that can destroy someone else's work**.

This plan reorders it: `rebase --autostash origin/HEAD` **before** the engine. The worktree is dirty, so git stashes, rebases, and pops. The tree comes back dirty and **already sitting on top of the remote's version of the base**. The engine then commits **once**, and the push is an ordinary fast-forward.

| Situation | Rebase position | Push |
|---|---|---|
| `ro push` alone, nothing committed yet | before the engine | **fast-forward, no force** |
| `ro push` after `ro commit`, remote unmoved | nothing to rebase | **fast-forward, no force** |
| `ro push` after `ro commit`, remote moved | after the commits | **`--force-with-lease`** |

`--force` — bare — is **never** used, in any row.

## The honest limit

Because `ro commit` is now a separate verb, a commit made at 10h and pushed at 12h, after the remote moved, **must** rewrite history. `--force-with-lease` is then required, not optional. Stating the limit is better than pretending the reordering makes force-push impossible.

## A failed autostash pop is a per-repo FAILURE

Never a proceed on a half-popped tree. Report it with the exact recovery: `git stash list`, `git stash pop`. Driving `stash`/`rebase`/`stash pop` as three steps ro controls itself would be the same thing with **three places to forget the cleanup** — exactly the failure class the credential design avoids by never rewriting a remote in the first place.

## The base comes from the repo, not from configuration

`git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` -> `origin/main`. One git command, no configuration, no GitHub API, correct for any clone. `--onto <BRANCH>` overrides it. There is no `[git] default_branch` key and no cached column: a cache of a branch name goes stale on a `main` -> `trunk` rename.

## Tests

- **The happy path never force-pushes.** A repo two commits behind with local changes: assert the recorded push argv contains **neither** `--force` **nor** `--force-with-lease`.
- A failed autostash pop is a per-repo failure naming the recovery, and **the engine is not dispatched** (assert the fake engine's invocation count is still zero).
- The recorded argv order is fetch -> rebase --autostash -> engine -> push.
- A remote whose HEAD is `origin/trunk` rebases onto `trunk`.
- After `ro commit` and then a moved remote, the push uses `--force-with-lease` and **never** bare `--force`.
acceptance_criteria: The happy-path push argv has no force flag. A failed autostash pop blocks the engine. The base is read from origin/HEAD. --force never appears.

title: Conflict resolution as a stage: agent edits, ro continues and pushes
description:
## The flow

```
push rejected
  -> rebase mechanically (no model)
     -> clean -> push                      the common case
     -> CONFLICT + --resolve -> engine, second dispatch, conflict prompt
        -> engine edits files and `git add`s what it resolved, then STOPS
        -> ro verifies the index, runs rebase --continue, pushes
     -> no --resolve -> show the conflicted paths, hand over
```

**There is no `ro conflict` verb.** It was proposed; an interactive command over twenty repos is not a command, which is the same rule that keeps `ro commit` from cloning mid-transaction.

## The split of labour, and why it is the whole point

- **The engine resolves the conflict.** Reads the conflicted files, decides what the resolution should be, edits the working tree, `git add`s what it resolved.
- **The engine does NOT run `rebase --continue`, and does NOT push.** ro does both, and only after **verifying the index is free of unmerged entries**. Running `--continue` with conflicts still present produces a second, more confusing failure, and the user learns to avoid the flag.
- **The second dispatch is a different call, not a retry.** Different prompt (*"resolve the conflicts in these paths; do not rebase, do not push"*), the same **stripped** environment, the same `RepoLock`.

The alternative — an agent that does the whole thing — is a tool where every identity guarantee is advice given to a process free to ignore it. The boundary does not relax because the situation got harder.

## `--resolve` is off by default

It is the only step where a model edits files mid-rebase. Default-off is not timidity: a model that resolves a conflict nobody had is worse than a stop, and the overwhelmingly common cause of a rejected push is a **stale branch** — three git commands that need no model at all.

`--yes` answers the rebase prompt automatically and **does not imply `--resolve`**: auto-rebasing is mechanical and safe to automate, auto-resolving a semantic conflict is not.

## Also: `abort` records the ref first

A tool that aborts a rebase has already thrown away commits unless the ref was captured first. Record the pre-operation HEAD, then abort, then **verify the ref matches**.

## Tests

- `--resolve` on a real conflict dispatches the engine exactly **once more**, with a different prompt, and the engine's captured output contains **no** `rebase --continue` and **no** `push**.
- A conflict **without** `--resolve` shows the paths and hands over; the engine is not dispatched.
- `--yes` alone does not enable `--resolve`.
- `abort` restores the recorded pre-operation ref — assert it equals the value captured before the rebase started.
acceptance_criteria: The engine edits and stages and stops. ro runs continue and push after verifying the index. --resolve is opt-in and --yes does not imply it. abort restores the recorded ref.

title: ro push refuses on a protected branch instead of inventing a name
description:
## The behaviour

```
$ ro push
error: main is a protected branch — `git checkout -b feat/x` first
```

**ro does not create a branch.** The old behaviour — silently create `ro/wip/<slug>-<run>` — existed **only to give a pull request something to point at**, and with PRs cut the reason is gone.

Naming a branch has consequences: it is what a teammate fetches, what appears in `git branch` next month, and what a later `ro push` assumes. The user is standing right there and can type it. A tool that invents a name is a tool that makes a decision with a blast radius on your behalf.

## The protected set

`is_protected_branch` is currently `[main, master, production, staging]` plus a `release/` prefix, matched **case-sensitively by exact equality** — so `Main` is not protected. **Normalize to case-insensitive**, keep at least `main` and `master`, and decide deliberately whether `production` and `staging` stay. That set is carried over from ro-sweep in Phase 4.

## `--onto` is the escape

For the rare case where the work belongs somewhere other than the default branch. That is the one real use the old PR base served, and it survives as a flag rather than a config key.

## Tests

- `ro push` on `main` refuses, names the fix, and **attempts no push** — assert the bare origin's reflog is unchanged.
- `Main` and `MASTER` are treated as protected (case-insensitivity).
- A feature branch pushes normally with `--set-upstream` on first push, and the second `ro push` needs no flag.
acceptance_criteria: Protected branches refuse with a named fix and no push attempt. The set is case-insensitive. A feature branch pushes normally and records its upstream.

title: ro sync: clone what is missing, fetch, pull --rebase
description:
## The pipeline — deliberately different from ship

```
ro sync --tag work
  targets: WHERE archived=0 AND disabled=0, filtered by --tag
  per repo, in parallel:
    working copy missing?  -> clone            (no engine, no branch, no commit)
    else                   -> git fetch
                              -> git pull --rebase  (or --strategy merge|ff-only)
                                 --autostash only if the flag was passed
    update the registry's last_synced_at
```

It must not touch the index or spawn anything.

## A dirty worktree is SKIPPED by default, not clobbered

This is where the old `--force` proposal was most dangerous. The correct answer is to say what happened and move on:

```
skipped: 3 uncommitted changes (use --autostash)
```

A fleet tool that discards uncommitted work because someone typed a flag **while rushing** is a tool that gets uninstalled after the first accident. There is no `--force` on this command; `--autostash` is the answer.

## Cloning here is safe

It is idempotent and the target is a known-empty path. What is **not** safe is discovering a typo'd local path partway through a commit-and-push loop and pulling a repository over the network to fill it — which is why `ro commit` and `ro push` skip an un-cloned row instead.

## Tests

- A registry row with no working copy is cloned; a row with one is fetched and pulled.
- A dirty worktree is skipped with the reason naming `--autostash`, and **nothing is written**.
- `--autostash` stashes, pulls, pops.
- `--strategy merge` and `ff-only` are honoured.
- An archived or disabled row is not pulled without `--include-archived`.
acceptance_criteria: Clone/fetch/pull work per row. A dirty worktree skips with a named reason and no write. --autostash round-trips. The archived/disabled filter applies.

title: Positional repo args and the ten-command flag surface
description:
## The surface

```
init  add  list  status  sync  commit  push  ship  doctor  config
```

Ten commands in three tiers: **daily** (sync, status, commit, push, ship), **registry** (add, list, doctor), **setup** (init, config). Plus `schema`.

**There is no `ro repos` namespace.** The regroup that moved six commands under one bought discoverability and cost muscle memory on the four most-used verbs in the tool; at this surface size a namespace disambiguates nothing.

## Flags that are NOT copied verbatim — and why

**No `ro sync --force`.** The proposal was "skip dirty check". A dirty worktree plus a *forced* pull is exactly where a forced operation destroys work: the plausible implementations are `git reset --hard` (throws away every uncommitted change in a repo nobody was looking at) or `git checkout -f` — same, quieter. This is a flag typed by someone who, by the premise of the tool, is **rushing**. The answer to a dirty worktree is `--autostash`. A tool whose whole premise is *"I am in a hurry across twenty repos"* should not have a flag that discards work faster than a human can read the help.

**`ro remove --delete` is gated, not removed.** Deleting a working copy is legitimate and is the only way to reclaim disk. It is also the exact operation that the Windows orphan bug would have aimed at **managed** repositories. So: refused without an interactive confirmation or `--non-interactive`; the full path printed before the prompt; the path re-checked against the registry immediately before `remove_dir_all`; and **a directory whose `.git` origin matches a *different* registered repo is refused outright** — that is a copy-paste accident, not a cleanup.

**`ro commit --amend` refuses when HEAD is already on the remote.** Amending a pushed commit rewrites history, and the next `ro push` would need `--force-with-lease` — a flag intended for *"I forgot a file"* can silently become a force-push. Guard with `git branch -r --contains HEAD` and say so in the error. Amending a purely local commit is free and stays.

**No global `--json`.** There is exactly one output selector, `--format text|json|ndjson`, per command. The codebase today has the opposite problem — a `toon` ValueEnum on one path and a free-form `--output json` String on another where only the literal `"json"` is honoured (`main.rs:1075`). A third spelling does not fix that, it entrenches it.

**No global `-q`/`-v`/`--quiet`/`--verbose`.** Both exist today and both are deleted: `cli.verbose` is read nowhere, and `cli.quiet` has a dead `let _quiet = cli.quiet;` at `main.rs:623` plus exactly one real read at `main.rs:704` — inside the `ro import` branch Phase 1 deletes. A verbosity flag nothing reads is a promise the tool does not keep.

**Consolidate the two duplicate `OutputFormat` enums** — `main.rs:22` had 3 variants, `ro-output/src/lib.rs:25` had 4, and the CLI used neither — into one.

## Also delete

`ro sync --resume` (there is no daemon to resume into). `ro repos scan`, `ro repos prune`, `ro repos update` as a verb, and `tag`/`untag`/`tags` — the `repo_tags` table has no writer and no reader today, and a feature with no consumer is the right thing to cut. `ro repos update` becomes `ro config set repos.<name>.<key>`.

## Tests

Every command in the tree is reachable and `ro --help` lists exactly the ten. `ro sync --force` **does not exist** — a test asserting the flag is rejected is how a well-meaning contributor does not add it back. `ro remove --delete` without confirmation is refused. `ro commit --amend` on a pushed HEAD is refused with a message naming the force-push consequence.
acceptance_criteria: Exactly ten commands, no namespace. --force does not exist on sync. remove --delete is gated and refuses a directory matching another registered repo. amend refuses on a pushed HEAD. No global --json or -q/-v. One OutputFormat enum remains.

title: Exit codes 0/1/2 and a distinct fatal path
description:
## The table

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **0** | every repo succeeded (and `--all` on an empty inventory is a legitimate 0) |
| **1** | partial — some repos succeeded, some did not |
| **2** | all failed |
| **64** | bad usage — an unknown flag, an unknown repo name, a name matching nothing, an invalid glob |
| **distinct** | a **fatal** error: bad config, `open_db` failure, a duplicate add. Not 1. |

## The collision that must be resolved

`2` currently means **clap usage error** in the existing code, and the fleet table wants `2 = all failed`. Any CI script keying on the old meaning silently reinterprets it. Release note required.

## The fatal path is a real gap

`main()` currently does:

```rust
if let Err(err) = run() { eprintln!("error: {err:?}"); std::process::exit(1); }
```

**Any escaped `anyhow::bail!` exits 1** — the same code the table assigns to *partial success*. A config file that will not parse is reported as "some repos succeeded", which is worse than a wrong number: it invites a retry that cannot work. Add a `FatalError` type mapped to its own code, and make the exit table enforceable rather than documented.

## `ro doctor` is not a fleet command

It keeps its own **0/1** (1 = some check failed), and its `Severity::Optional` probes can **never** move the exit code. `ro repos prune` hard-exits **3** (`main.rs:812`). State this in the docs, or a reader applies the fleet table to every command and misreads a failed environment check as a partial run.

## Tests

Every commit succeeded and every push failed is **not 0** — this is the current bug at `main.rs`. A bad usage is 64, not 2. A fatal config error is neither 0, 1, nor 2.
acceptance_criteria: 0/1/2 fleet outcomes, 64 usage, a distinct fatal code. A fatal config error does not exit 1. ro doctor and prune document their own codes. Every row of the table has a test.

title: The per-repo summary is the audit trail — and run history stays unwired
description:
## What replaces the audit trail

Every run prints one line per repo naming **branch, engine, the account the credential resolved to, commit count, and result**:

```
feat/retry-extraction   repo_orchestrator   claude   3 commits   pushed   fast-forward
voice-ai-dashboard      company  (me@corp.com)         1 commit   pushed   fast-forward
cass                    personal (me@gmail.com)       2 commits   CONFLICT resolved  pushed
repo_orchestrator — clean, skipped
```

Plus the NDJSON form under `--format ndjson` for anyone who wants to pipe it somewhere.

## Run history is NOT wired — say so in the code

`ro_jobs::open_run` / `append_event` / `finalize_run` have **zero production callers** today. They exist, they are tested, and nothing calls them, which is exactly the kind of thing that looks like a feature and is not one.

With no `ro run` verb there is nothing to read the rows with, and **a database nobody queries is not an audit trail**. So: **do not wire them.** Put a comment on each saying why, so the next contributor does not helpfully connect them.

## What is lost, stated plainly rather than discovered later

This answers *"what did ro do to this repo"*. It does **not** answer *"what did ro push last Tuesday, with which account"* — a fleet tool that pushes with your credentials and leaves no record is a tool you will be afraid to run unattended. That gap is named here and in the plan's summary, not hidden behind a table nobody queries.

**Run history is the first thing to add back**, and the tables already exist.

## The NDJSON envelope

`NdjsonEvent { kind, ts, #[serde(flatten)] payload }` moves verbatim from the deleted `ro-output` crate into `crates/ro/src/ndjson.rs`, with the surviving `ndjson.rs` tests. Vocabulary redrawn for the fleet: `run_start`, `repo_scanned`, `repo_skipped`, `lock_acquired`, `safety_blocked`, `branch_created`, `engine_dispatch`, `engine_timeout`, `rebase_started`, `rebase_conflict`, `rebase_resolved`, `push_ok`, `push_failed`, `run_end`.

**Every line carries a non-null `ts`.** Today the production path emits `"ts": null` on every line — the old code used bare `serde_json::to_string` at `main.rs:1092,1100,1108` and never went through the writer that stamps it.

## Ordering is deterministic

`--format ndjson` and `-j 4` produce the **same event ordering** as `-j 1` for the same fleet. The coordinator drains outcomes **in target order, not completion order**.

## Text output

Hand-rolled `println!` per command handler, which is what happens today. **The plan does not build a shared text renderer** — state it so nobody hunts for one that does not exist.
acceptance_criteria: One summary line per repo naming branch, engine, account, commits, result. Every NDJSON line has a non-null ts. -j 4 and -j 1 produce the same ordering. open_run/append_event/finalize_run remain unwired with a comment saying why.

title: Add a test that every ro command named in README/FEATURES exists in the clap tree
description:
## The recurring failure this exists to stop

Three times in one session, removing a command left the documentation describing it:

- `ro import` survived in the `generate_robot_docs` JSON literal, in three README
  quickstart blocks, and as a full flag table in FEATURES.md
- `ro self-update` survived in five places, including a README FAQ section whose
  entire body was two invocations of the removed command
- one of those was a **near-miss introduced by me**: the line was removed, then
  `git checkout HEAD -- main.rs` (to undo an over-deletion) restored it, and the
  omission was not re-applied before pushing

**Nothing in the build or the test suite catches any of these.** A command name in
a markdown table, or in a hand-written `json!` literal, is not compiled and not
executed. Every one of them was found by grep, or by a reviewer reading the diff.
With six more commands coming out in this phase — `fork`, `health`, `review`,
the rest of `sweep`, `robot-docs` — the same manual grep runs six more times, and
the odds of it being skipped on the last one are not good.

## The test

Read every `ro <word>` and `ro <word> <sub>` out of `README.md` and
`FEATURES.md`, and assert each one exists in the clap tree. `clap::CommandFactory`
is already a dependency and `ro schema` is being built from it, so the live
command list is available to the test with no new plumbing.

Direction matters and only one direction is useful:

- **docs -> tree** is the one that catches this. A documented command that no
  longer exists is a broken promise to a human or an agent.
- **tree -> docs** would fail for every command the docs happen not to mention,
  which is a documentation-style opinion, not a correctness property. Do not
  assert it.

So: the test is `every command named in the docs is a real command`, not
`every command is documented`.

## What it will and will not catch

It catches a removed command still advertised anywhere in those two files. It
does not catch a wrong flag, a wrong description, or a command documented with
the wrong subcommand. That is fine — the goal is to make the recurring,
mechanical, invisible failure class impossible rather than to complete, and this
is the cheapest possible test that removes the largest number of manual greps.

## Why this is not the same as bead ro-1bo.7

`ro-1bo.7` replaces `generate_robot_docs` with `ro schema` so the *machine*`
surface cannot drift. This is the *human* surface. They are the same root cause
with two consumers, and fixing only the machine one leaves every markdown table
uncovered.

## Placement

Phase 1, and deliberately early in the cut sequence rather than at the end. Its
value is proportional to how many removals it has already been present for; a
guard added after the cuts have shipped has nothing left to catch.
design: Integration or unit test in crates/ro/tests. Reads the two markdown files, extracts `ro <cmd>` tokens, checks against the clap tree via CommandFactory. Runs in CI on all three OSes like the rest of the suite.
acceptance_criteria: A test parses command names out of README.md and FEATURES.md and asserts each exists in the clap tree. It fails when a command is removed without its docs being updated. The reverse direction (every command is documented) is deliberately not asserted.
notes: Motivated by three consecutive doc-drift near-misses in one session, none of which the build or the existing tests could see. P0 because the remaining Phase 1 cuts will each need a manual grep otherwise.
close_reason: crates/ro/tests/cli_docs_match.rs is in place and green. It parses 'ro --help' rather than importing the clap tree, because ro is a binary crate with no lib target, and asserts one direction only: every command the docs name must exist in the tree.
